extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of sociology, political theory, criminology, and legal theory
extracted.subtask_short: theory of law and the capitalist state
extracted.subtask_description: Analytical criteria for relating law, crime and social control to the capitalist state from a Marxist/Gramscian perspective; addresses historical specificity, relative autonomy, hegemony, and the dual mechanisms of coercion and consent. Useful for developing or evaluating theoretical accounts of state, law and crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'control-culture' approach adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the 'control-culture' approach locates centres of power historically, differentiates between types of state or political regime, specifies the social formation that establishes a particular legal order, and examines repressive functions in relation to consensual functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticises the control-culture approach as 'too imprecise' because it 'identifies centres of power and their importance' but 'does not locate them historically', 'does not differentiate adequately between different types of state or political regime', and 'does not examine the repressive functions of the state apparatuses in relation to their consensual functions'. Use these failings as negative indicators when assessing such an approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Situate law/crime in relation to the capitalist state and class struggle
rubrics_metrics.description: Frame questions of law, crime, social control, consent, legitimacy and opposition explicitly in relation to the capitalist state and the class struggle rather than in abstract or ahistorical terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors insist that issues of legality and illegality 'belong... to the question of the capitalist state and the class struggle' and that law is 'centrally connected' with modes of hegemony in bourgeois social formations. Theoretical accounts should therefore connect legal institutions and criminality to class relations and state forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical specificity of state forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate the historical specificity of the state form under analysis (e.g., post-laissez-faire/Welfare State, fully developed parliamentary democracy) and locate significant moments of shift and change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns against non-historicized concepts: the state must be located 'at a specific historical conjuncture' and moment(s) of crisis and change must be identified. Avoid generic, ahistorical uses of 'the state'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop a fully elaborated Marxist theory of the state
rubrics_metrics.description: Where drawing on Marxism, avoid simple or reductive formulae; work out the elements of a Marxist theory of the state (rather than using basic slogans) in light of contemporary developments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note 'there is no fully elaborated theory of this kind to be found in Marx and Engels' and that 'the elements... require... to be worked out'. Assessments should therefore test for the depth and specificity of Marxist theorization rather than superficial appeals to Marx or Engels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain 'uneven correspondence' / relative autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the non-simple, non-immediate correspondence between the mode of production (economic base) and legal/political/ideological forms (superstructure), i.e., their 'relative autonomy' and 'uneven' relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text emphasises Marx's and Poulantzas's insistence on 'relative autonomy' and the 'uneven correspondence' between economic development and law/state. Analyses should show how legal/juridical forms relate unevenly to economic structures and avoid deterministic base-superstructure readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative specificity of legal forms to productive development
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that legal codes and juridical forms adapt differently to capitalist development in different national contexts (e.g., Code Civil vs. Prussian law), and include comparative/historical specificity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engels' examples (e.g., 'classic law code of bourgeois society' like the Code Civil suiting France but ill-adapted to Prussia) are cited to argue that legal forms must be analysed in relation to the specifics of national productive development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain the state's dual character (product of class antagonisms yet appearing independent)
rubrics_metrics.description: Explain how the state is both produced by class antagonisms and at the same time appears as an independent, universal authority that moderates class conflict.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Marx/Lenin/Gramsci, the text stresses this paradox: the state 'gives [the ruling class's] will... a universal expression' while being 'the product and manifestation of the irreconcilability of class antagonisms'. Theorists should account for both sides of this duality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'appearance' / representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat 'appearances' (political, legal, ideological forms) as representations that exist and have effects but can mask deeper relations; analysis should distinguish surface effects from underlying social relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors clarify Marx's use of 'appearance' as a theory of darstellung/representation: 'appearances... are false, not because they do not exist, but because they invite us to mistake surface effects for real relations.' Use this lens to read legal and political phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show how juridical/political forms conceal production relations (use analogies like the wage-form)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrate how forms in the sphere of circulation (wage-form, commodity/money forms) and juridical/political appearances veil the underlying relations of production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter uses the wage-form and circulation to illustrate how exchange forms 'hide the play of [capital's] inner mechanism'. Apply analogous arguments to how law/state forms can obscure exploitation and class relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use concrete historical case studies of political crises
rubrics_metrics.description: Ground theoretical claims about state forms and their relative autonomy in detailed historical analysis of political crises (e.g., Marx's Eighteenth Brumaire) to show how class compositions and mode-of-production constraints shape state outcomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Eighteenth Brumaire is offered as an 'object lesson' in uneven correspondence: assessments should explain how the stage of productive development and the combination of class forces set limits on political resolutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess the state's role in social reproduction and conforming civil society
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate how the state functions as an instrument that shapes social and cultural life to favour capitalist production and the reproduction of capitalist social relations (legal codes, education, cultural apparatuses, family, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting Gramsci, the state is 'the instrument for conforming civil society to the economic structure'. Analyses should examine state control over education, culture, legal codes and other institutions that reproduce labour power and ideology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for both coercion and consent mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyse the state's simultaneous use of coercion (law, legal institutions, reserve coercive force) and consent (leadership, education, cultural direction) as interdependent mechanisms of rule.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gramsci's distinction is central: coercion is a necessary face of the state, but the state works best through leadership and consent (the 'armour of consent'). Evaluations should trace how coercive apparatuses and consent-producing cultural/political apparatuses operate together.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate the legal system's dual (repressive and educative) role
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise the law as both the repressive, punitive aspect of the state's activity and as a positive educative function that shapes moral norms and uses public opinion as sanction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states 'The Law is the repressive and negative aspect of the entire positive, civilizing activity undertaken by the State' and gives examples of punishment/reward and use of public opinion. Analyses should capture both dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mechanisms for achieving hegemony (political representation and civil society)
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify and evaluate mechanisms by which a dominant class extends authority into civil society and the state—representation, parties, trade unions, employers' federations, public opinion, cultural organisations—forming a 'historical bloc'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gramsci's account is cited: hegemony is achieved through political representation, organisational sway over private associations, education and cultural institutions. Assessments should examine these concrete mechanisms and their capacity to 'cement' consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: State as mediator imposing compromises and limits on ruling-class interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Examine how the state may extract political/economic 'costs' from dominant groups to secure consent and social cohesion, and how such compromises must not touch the fundamental economic essentials of hegemony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues the state can 'impose these political costs on narrower ruling-class interests' and that hegemony 'presupposes that account be taken of the interests... of the groups over which hegemony is exercised'. Evaluate the extent and limits of such mediation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid reducing the state to 'executive committee of the ruling class'
rubrics_metrics.description: Reject simplistic readings that treat the state merely as a direct instrument of a single ruling class fraction; instead analyse the state's relative autonomy and mediating role among class fractions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors caution that the phrase obscures the state's specificity under capitalism: for example the industrial bourgeoisie in 19th-century England 'ruled' through a Parliament dominated by the landed aristocracy. Theorists should pay attention to mediation, alliances and ruling fractions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include institutions of social reproduction in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporate the family, education system, cultural apparatuses and forms of consumption into analyses of how labour power is reproduced and how ideological conformity is produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter discusses the reproduction of labour power via the family/consumption (living wage), education (skills/knowledge) and cultural apparatuses (morality, civic conscience). Evaluations should trace these non-productive spheres as essential to capitalist reproduction and state strategy.
